OPEN MIND hyperMILL CAD/CAM Python OPEN MIND hyperMILL CAD/CAM Python 0.9.0.53897 - 2024-04-16 (C) Copyright 2020-2024 OPEN MIND Technologies AG Argelsrieder Feld 5 82234 Wessling Germany www.openmind-tech.com hyperMILL CAD Python API How to start Python is delivered as an embedded system together with OPEN MIND hyperMILL CAD/CAM, you do not need to install a separate Python installation on your workstation. Indeed, if you have another Python installation running, we cannot guarantee that hyperMILL Python will run out-of-the-box. OPEN MIND hyperMILL CAD/CAM Python (short OM Python) uses Visual Studio Code (aka VS Code) as the development environment to edit and debug Python scripts. Before continuing, make sure you have installed VS Code. VS Code installation OPEN MIND hyperMILL CAD/CAM Python is optimized to work with Microsoft Visual Studio Code (code.visualstudio.com/Download). VS Code exists also as a portable solution that does not need any installation. More about portable VS Code is here: code.visualstudio.com/docs/editor/portable -- 1 of 389 -- VS Code works in directory structure, all settings and extensions are created below the main directory. This is very convenient, if you are working with different projects. All configuration settings are saved in a folder .vscode. The Python browser (see Python Window) can automatically generate a .vscode folder with an appropriate configuration. After the first start of VS Code, the user will be guided through a optional wizard. For example, the user can install an optional language pack. -- 2 of 389 -- Open first the folder that is containing the project (+, +). Remark: For debugging it seems to be substantially that you open the folder, where the source code is located. Now you can create a new Python file or select an existing Python file. VS Code recognizes the file format (bottom-right corner shows Python) and wants to install a necessary extensions. Otherwise you have to install Python extension manually, for example “Python extension for Visual Studio Code” from Microsoft. If you have opened an existing file, you will see a lot of errors in the source code. VS Code can switch between different Python installations, and it is likely that the wrong installations is chosen. -- 3 of 389 -- To use the full intellisense support, one has to use the right interpreter installation. The selection is done by the command key shortcut ++

. Now you get into the VS Code command window, where you have to search for “Python: Select interpreter” or “Python: Interpreter auswählen”. VS Code suggests a list of found Python interpreters. The OM Python interpreter can be normally found here: C:\Program Files\OPEN MIND\Shared\\Python\Python.exe. If the interpreter is not shown, you can add it manually with “+ Enter interpreter path…”. Warning: Selecting a wrong interpreter is a common source of errors! We are using Embedded Python, all information are stored in one directory. This ensure that we can deliver an own Python for each hyperMILL version. Intellisense OM Python has an integrated help and support for intellisense in Visual Studio Code and other IDEs. -- 4 of 389 -- Warning: If the intellisense does not work, check that you have selected the right Python interpreter inside VS Code. Python Window Utility buttons In the Python window we can identify three areas. Utility buttons It contains the button to open the documentation, open a cmd to manage the python interpreter and open the python options. Python browser -- 5 of 389 -- It shows all your Python projects and scripts. You can edit and run them. Output It contains the script execution output. Python options Through the corresponding button you can open the Python options. -- 6 of 389 -- Let’s see what they are, if and when it is necessary to change their value Python executable folder Readonly. It is the path to the HM Python interpreter. Visual Studio Code folder It is the path of the VS Code installation foder, where Code.exe is placed. You may need to change the value if you installed VS Code to a different location than the default. User workspace folder This folder contents the scripts you see in the projects browser when ‘User’ is the selected root. Change the value when you want to work on Python projects placed in a different location on the file system. User template folder You can place in this folder Python scripts that you can use as a starting script when creating a new project. When you want to create a new project, the context menu will have an additional item for each existing script template. TCP port for debug This is a port used by the application to communicate with VS Code. If the default port is not available (another process is using it), change it to an available one. You should consider changing the port if the debug is not working as expected. -- 7 of 389 -- Clean output at run If checked, the script output area is cleaned at every run. At the bottom you find the three buttons to restore the installation settings (Reset), save the modified settings (Save) or eestore the last saved settings (Load). Python browser The browser shows all the Python projects present in a particular folder of the file system. At the top you can choose to work in the current user folder “User” or take inspiration from the from the numerous ready-to-use examples by selecting “Samples”. To view and manage the contents of a different User folder on the file system, you can change the path to this folder at any time through Python options. In addition to viewing your Python projects (and the scripts inside), the browser also helps you manage them. You can create/rename a folder Mostly important you can: Create new VS Code Python projects (via context menu) -- 8 of 389 -- Create new Python scripts inside an existing project (via context menu) Select which is the start-up script of a project (via context menu) Editing you scripts (via context menu, double click or Edit button) -- 9 of 389 -- To write and edit scripts, the application will open the corresponding Python project in an instance of VS Code. Warning: If OPEN MIND hyperMILL CAD/CAM cannot open VS Code, open the Python options and make sure the VS Code installation path is correct (that’s where you find Code.exe). Once your Python script is ready, you can launch it into execution by selecting the corresponding project (the one containing the script) and pressing “Run”. You can also launch it via context menu. While the script is running the application is frozen, the user cannot interact with it, but any model update is shown in the graphic area and any output message is shown in the window below. The control returns to the user as soon as the script finishes. -- 10 of 389 -- Note: There are ways to stop the execution of a script and resume it after a certain action. For example, using Python you can open a command or a custom dialog and wait for it to close. Python projects When you create a new Python project, a folder is created in the file system. This folder will have a default name (which can be modified at any time). You will find inside the project a single Python script having the same name as the folder (which can also be modified). Inside the folder there are also two hidden subfolders, .om and .vscode, containing information for the correct functioning of the Python window and VS Code. Warning: Remember not to delete or modify the contents of these .om and .vscode folders. You can open the corresponding file system location. -- 11 of 389 -- After the project creation, you can manage it through the Python browser, or you can add/delete/renaming scripts directly via file system. As already explained, the HM Python browser is a window on the file system: any changes you make on it will automatically be visible on HM. Warning: Do not create a full new project in the file system by hand. You should always create projects through the Python browser, since HM needs the .om and .vscode folders to function properly. If you need to create a new project by hand, remember to copy these folders from an existing one. OM Python always uses VS Code as editor for your script. When you double click on a script in the browser, the full Python project where the selected script belongs will be open in VS Code. Note: You cannot create a script not belonging to any project. If you receive a Python script from someone else and want to run it on your hm, just create a new project via the browser and paste the contents of the script into the script of the project. You can also manually copy the script file directly into the project folder and set the file as start-up. If you receive a full Python project, just copy and paste inside your user folder. Installing third-party Python packages In Python, “package” and “library” are often used interchangeably, referring to a collection of modules that provide related functionality. Python is one of the most used programming languages in the world. There are -- 12 of 389 -- thousands of libraries out there ready to be used. Sometimes you will need to install them in order to get the result you want from your scripts. General remarks You (the end user) can install additional third-party Python packages on own risk! OPEN MIND does not provide any support for third-party packages. Some third-party packages might fail to install. You might need additional rights for the following steps. Please contact your IT administrator first. Check the PATH environment variable Important: The OM Python installation path should never be added to the Windows PATH environment variable! OM Python installations are designed to work side-by-side. Each installation works with it’s own Python environment. If python.exe is in the PATH environment, there might be unpredictable behaviour, because a wrong Python interpreter is used or packages are installed at a wrong place. Best practice: Remove all Python folders from the PATH variable! Using pip In Python, you typically use package managers such as pip or conda to install external packages. Installing an external library on OM Python interpreter is fairly easy. 1. Open a terminal through the button 2. Run the following command pip install --user or pip install --trusted-host pypi.org --trusted-host files.pythonhoste Replace with the name of the package you want to install. It’s strongly recommended to use the option --user. The parameters --trusted-host are optional. They are required in some networks to download packages with self-signed certificates. If you want to uninstall a package, just substitute ‘install’ with ‘uninstall’ pip uninstall After installation, you can import and use the installed packages in your Python scripts. See also pip --help for more information. Working with requirement files For more than one package or for existing projects, it’s possible to save all required packages to a requirement file, normally named requirements.txt. This text file can be found also in many open source -- 13 of 389 -- projects. Example: ###### Requirements without Version Specifiers ###### nose nose-cov beautifulsoup4 ###### Requirements with Version Specifiers ###### docopt == 0.6.1 # Version Matching. Must be version 0.6.1 keyring >= 4.1.1 # Minimum version 4.1.1 coverage != 3.5 # Version Exclusion. Anything except version 3.5 Mopidy-Dirble ~= 1.1 # Compatible release. Same as >= 1.1, == 1.* Start pip with the -r option to read the packages from the text file, e.g. .\python -m pip install -r requirements.txt --user --trusted-host pypi.org --trusted-host files.py Python virtual environments Users that might use different project with different package requirements, might have a look at Python virtual environments. A virtual environment can store dependencies for each Python project independently. Details can be found here: https://docs.Python.org/3.11/library/venv.html How to debug scripts During your work with Python, it will often happen that the result of a script is not the desired one, either because the execution raises a strange error, or because there is no trace of the cylinder you built in your script. If you are taking your first steps on Python, a simple and effective way to better understand the malfunction of your script is to add print statements in order to see where and why the script does not do what you expect. In Python, like many other languages, you can print not only strings but also the content of your variables. # Define a function that adds two numbers def add_numbers(a, b): print("Inside add_numbers function") # Debugging message print("Adding", a, "and", b) # Debugging message return a + b # Call the add_numbers function result = add_numbers(3, 5) # Print the result print("The result is:", result) # Debugging message In addition to the print function, you could use many other features, such as opening a MessageBox or writing to a file. All of these approaches are great, but sometimes you will need to stop the execution of your script at a certain point and debug it step by step. As in most programming languages, this is also possible in Python. To do this 1. Open the script you want to debug on VS Code via the Python Window. 2. Add breakpoint 3. Start a debugging session. Use the “Debug” button on the “Run and Debug” sidebar to start a debugging session and select “Python: Remote Attach”. -- 14 of 389 -- Don’t use the the Start/Debug button on the right side. Warning: When you want to debug a script, remember to open it through the Python browsers, and not directly on VS Code. VS Code HyperMillExtension If you have problem in debugging your script, ensure that you have the VS Code HyperMillExtension installed. To check if the VS Code has the estension installed and enabled: * Start the OPEN MIND hyperMILL CAD/CAM application * Open a projetc from Python browser * Check if in the extensions the HyperMillExtension is installed. If HyperMillExtension is not installed, you shuold install it manually. Open the Extensions browser (see also VS Code installation) and install the Python extension. In the Extension Browser top select ‘…’ (Views and More actions) - -- 15 of 389 -- Install from VSIX and select the file. The extension is located in <…>\Shared\ \Python\hypermillextension-1.0.0.vsix (see VS Code HyperMillExtension) The HyperMillExtension is installed. OPEN MIND Coding Style We recommend writing application scripts using PEP 8 coding style. “How to Write Beautiful Python Code With PEP 8” is a good article to introduce PEP8. It begins: “PEP 8 exists to improve the readability of Python code. But why is readability so important? Why is writing readable code one of the guiding principles of the Python language, according to the Zen of Python? As Guido van Rossum said, “Code is read much more often than it is written.” You may spend a few minutes, or a whole day, writing a piece of code to process user authentication. Once you’ve written it, you’re never going to write it again. But you’ll definitely have to read it again. That piece of code might remain part of a project you’re working on. Every time you go back to that file, you’ll have to remember what that code does and why you wrote it, so readability matters. If you’re new to Python, it can be difficult to remember what a piece of code does a few days, or weeks, after you wrote it. If you follow PEP 8, you can be sure that you’ve named your variables well. You’ll know that you’ve added enough whitespace so it’s easier to follow logical steps in your code. You’ll also have commented your code well. All this will mean your code is more readable and easier to come back to. As a beginner, following the rules of PEP 8 can make learning Python a much more pleasant task. Following PEP 8 is particularly important if you’re looking for a development job. Writing clear, readable code shows professionalism. It’ll tell an employer that you understand how to structure your code well. If you have more experience writing Python code, then you may need to collaborate with others. Writing readable code here is crucial. Other people, who may have never met you or seen your coding style before, will have to read and understand your code. Having guidelines that you follow and recognize will make it easier for others to read your code.” References PEP 8 - Style Guide for Python Code How to Write Beautiful Python Code With PEP 8 Zen of Python An inspiration for you to write beautiful scripts: -- 16 of 389 -- Beautiful is better than ugly. Explicit is better than implicit. Simple is better than complex. Complex is better than complicated. Flat is better than nested. Sparse is better than dense. Readability counts. Special cases aren’t special enough to break the rules. Although practicality beats purity. Errors should never pass silently. Unless explicitly silenced. In the face of ambiguity, refuse the temptation to guess. There should be one– and preferably only one –obvious way to do it. Although that way may not be obvious at first unless you’re Dutch. Now is better than never. Although never is often better than right now. If the implementation is hard to explain, it’s a bad idea. If the implementation is easy to explain, it may be a good idea. Namespaces are one honking great idea – let’s do more of those! OM Python User Manual In short we will explain the main concepts of OM Python API. By reading this manual you will have an overview of the potential of OM Python, starting from the key concepts and ending with complete examples of real use cases. OM Python Package OM Python Package is no different from any other python package available out there. The package consists of a series of modules and subpackages, each of which represents a specific semantic area of the software. The image below represents the OM Python package structure. -- 17 of 389 -- In the API documentation you will find a deep view for each module and subpackage. For now let’s briefly descrive the most important ones. om.math. It contains the basic mathematical objects, like om.math.Point3d, om.math.Axis3d and om.math.Vector3d. om.cad. It contains the CAD object model, i.e. all the objects (with related functions) to know and manage your CAD entities. om.cam. It contains the CAM object model, i.e. all the objects (with related functions) to know and manage your CAM jobs. om.commands. It contains a function for each command available in the HM menu bars. Current Document One need you will have in almost every script will be to get a reference to the current open document in HM. Once you have the current document, you will be able to know all its cad and cam features, as well as perform all necessary operations on it. Basic example how to get cad and cam model from the current document. import om import om.cad.core import om.cam.core # get the application instance app: om.Application = om.Application() # get the current document document: om.Document = app.CurrentDocument # read the document name document_name: str = document.Name # get the cad and cam models # from them you have access to all cad and cam information cad_model: om.cad.core.CadModel = document.CadModel cad_model: om.cam.core.CamModel = document.CamModel -- 18 of 389 -- Although getting the reference to the current document is essential for most scripts, many useful actions do not assume an open document. Some actions that can be performed without an open document are: creating a new document, opening an existing one, importing external formats and changing options. Basic Geometry Inside the om.math module you will find all the basic mathematical and geometric objects. You will use this class in many higher-level APIs. These are the classes you will find in the module. Objects om.math.Coord3d om.math.Point3d om.math.Vector3d om.math.UnitVector3d om.math.Box3d om.math.Axis3d om.math.Coord2d om.math.Vector2d om.math.UnitVector2d om.math.Box2d om.math.Axis2d om.math.Plane om.math.Interval om.math.Transformation3d om.math.Similarity3d om.math.RigidMotion3d This following script shows how to express a point in a different reference system by combining matrices. We have two different workplanes, wpA and wpB. We have a point with coordinate expressed in the wpA reference system. We want to calcolate the point in the wpB reference system. Express a point in another reference system. import om import om.cad.core cad_model = om.Application().CurrentDocument.CadModel wp_man = cad_model.WorkplanesManager # get the wpA reference system object ref_sys_A: om.cad.core.ReferenceSystem = wp_man.GetReferenceSystemByName("wpA") # get the wpB reference system object ref_sys_B: om.cad.core.ReferenceSystem = wp_man.GetReferenceSystemByName("wpB") # get the World to A transformation matrix rigid_motion_W_to_A = ref_sys_A.Motion # get the World to B transformation matrix rigid_motion_W_to_B = ref_sys_B.Motion # combine the matrices to get the A to B transformation matrix rigid_motion_A_to_B = rigid_motion_W_to_B.Inverse() * rigid_motion_W_to_A # define a point in wpA coordinates pt_A = [75.0, 10.0, 0.0] # calculate the point coordinates in wpB pt_B = rigid_motion_A_to_B * pt_A print(pt_B) Commands When you use OPEN MIND hyperMILL CAD/CAM, you make most changes to the model through the commands available in the various menus. Whether you want to open a new model, create a new profile or -- 19 of 389 -- assign a tag to an entity, what you need to do is open the right command dialog, modify the parameters and execute the command. 1. Open the command you want to use. 2. Change the parameters. In this case we have selected the circle as the base curve of our sweep, and we checked the “With bases” and “Solid” checkbox to obtain a solid with bases. 3. Execute the command. After apply we get new entities in our model. The new entities are also visible in the model window on the right (solid of id 11 with its faces). -- 20 of 389 -- We mapped the menu commands into a specific sub-package, om.commands. For each menu we have e dedicated module. There is a 1-1 relationship between menu and module. Note: The module has the same name of the menu. Menu om.commands module File file Edit edit Select select Drafting drafting Curves curves Shapes shapes Booleans boolean Modify modify View view Workplane workplane Tags tags Analysis analysis Electrodes electrodes Within these modules each command is represented by a function. Similarly to the menu-module, there is often a 1-1 relationship between command and function as well. Again, similarly to the menu-module, the name of the function always recalls what you see in the menu. In some cases a command has been mapped to multiple functions in order to simplify its use for the python developer. For example, many commands have a Mode parameter, and each mode has unique parameters. In these cases the command could present a different function for each mode. -- 21 of 389 -- At the end of the day, since the structure and names of the python API derive from the structure of the software you use every day, finding the rigth function is very simple. Even the parameter names recall those you see in the command dialog. Note: To find the function corresponding to a command present in an HM menu, search in the corresponding python module for a function with a similar name. Import an external format file import om.commands.file # get the default .igs open settings igs_settings: om.cad.core.PropertyBag = om.commands.file.GetOpenSettings("igs") # do not import the points igs_settings["igs_EF_Points"] = False # import the .igs file with custom settings document: om.Document = om.commands.file.OpenDocument( r"C:\temp\Model_0.igs", settings=igs_settings ) Boolean operation between two solids import om.commands.booleans solid_a = om.commands.select.GetEntityById(1) solid_b = om.commands.select.GetEntityById(8) warnings = [] solids_result = om.commands.booleans.CreateBooleanDifference( solid_a, solid_b, warnings = warnings # if the command fails you can read its warnings ) All commands share the same last optional parameter: warnings In cases where the command does not produce the desired result (for example the desired entities are not created), you can pass an empty list to the function. The list will be populated with the warnings: these are the same informations that you would see in the HM info window. Show command -- 22 of 389 -- Under the package om.cad you find an additional gui module. Inside you find the ShowCommand() function which accepts the name of a command function as first arguments. You can use this function to open a command dialog. Note: When a command dialog is open through ShowCommand(), the script is blocked up until the dialog is up. As soon as the dialog is closed the script resumes its execution. Show command example import om.commands.booleans import om.cad.gui import om.commands.tags # create a new boolean tag tag = om.commands.tags.CreateBooleanTag( "PYTHON_SOLID", defaultValue=True ) # show the boolean difference command dialog # this stop the script execution up until the dialog is not closed solids_result = om.cad.gui.ShowCommand( om.commands.booleans.CreateBooleanDifference ) # apply the tag to the boolean result for ent in solids_result: om.commands.tags.AssignTag( tag, entities=solids_result ) The ShowCommand() function has also a kwargs argument to pre-populate the command with your parameter values. The parameters are the same you find in the standard command function. Note: When you call the Show, all the command parameters become optional. The example below is the same as before, but we pre-populate the command dialog with the solidA parameter. Pre-populate the command dialog import om.commands.booleans import om.cad.gui import om.commands.tags tag = om.commands.tags.CreateBooleanTag( "PYTHON_SOLID", defaultValue=True ) # show the boolean difference command dialog with a pre-populated parameter solids_result = om.cad.gui.ShowCommand( om.commands.booleans.CreateBooleanDifference, solidA = om.commands.select.GetEntitiesById(3) ) for ent in solids_result: om.commands.tags.AssignTag( tag, entities=solids_result ) You can decide to populate some parameters of the via python command, open the command dialog with these parameters set, change the remaining parameters directly on HM and apply the command by hand. Note: When you call the ShowCommand(), the result of the function is the one from the last apply. -- 23 of 389 -- Object construction To use the library is important to understand how the objects can be created. Many times, it is possible to create an object using different types of parameters. Lets take for example the class Coord3d. It has nine different constructors: Parameter types Description no parameters Creates the Coord3d object with default values [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] float, float, float Creates the Coord3d object with given coordinates om.math.Coord3d Creates the Coord3d copy of another Coord3d om.math.Vector3d Creates the Coord3d given a Vector3d om.math.UnitVector3d Creates the Coord3d given a UnitVector3d sequence[float] Creates the Coord3d given a array (sequence) of float om.math.Point3d Creates the Coord3d given a Point3d om.cad.core.GeomEntity Creates the Coord3d object from an entity om.cad.core.Point Creates the Coord3d object from a ParPoint The code below shows all these constructors in action. coord = om.math.Coord3d() coord = om.math.Coord3d(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) coord = om.math.Coord3d(om.math.Coord3d(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) coord = om.math.Coord3d(om.math.Vector3d(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) coord = om.math.Coord3d(om.math.UnitVector3d(1.0, 0.0, 0.0)) coord = om.math.Coord3d([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) coord = om.math.Coord3d(om.math.Point3d(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) coord = om.math.Coord3d(om.commands.select.GetEntityById(9)) coord = om.math.Coord3d(om.cad.core.Point(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) When the number of constructors is high, to simplify the usage of the library we have added static methods with a talking name that can be used to create the objects. The name of the methods starts with the prefix “CreateFrom” followed by the types of parameters or the name is “CreateDefault” if there are not parameters. For example, to create the Coord3d there are nine different static methods: Name method Description CreateDefault() Creates the Coord3d object with default values [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] CreateFromComponents() Creates the Coord3d object with given coordinates CreateFromCoord3d() Creates a Coord3d given another Coord3d CreateFromVector3d() Creates the Coord3d given a Vector3d CreateFromUnitVector3d() Creates the Coord3d given a UnitVector3d CreateFromArray() Creates the Coord3d given a array (sequence) of float CreateFromGeomPoint() Creates the Coord3d given a Point3d CreateFromGeomEntity() Creates the Coord3d object from an entity CreateFromParPoint() Creates the Coord3d object from a ParPoint This snippet produces the same result of the snippet above. coord = om.math.Coord3d.CreateDefault() coord = om.math.Coord3d.CreateFromComponents(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) coord = om.math.Coord3d.CreateFromCoord3d(om.math.Coord3d(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) coord = om.math.Coord3d.CreateFromVector3d(om.math.Vector3d(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) coord = om.math.Coord3d.CreateFromUnitVector3d(om.math.UnitVector3d(1.0, 0.0, 0.0)) coord = om.math.Coord3d.CreateFromArray([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) coord = om.math.Coord3d.CreateFromGeomPoint(om.math.Point3d(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) -- 24 of 389 -- coord = om.math.Coord3d.CreateFromGeomEntity(om.commands.select.GetEntityById(9)) coord = om.math.Coord3d.CreateFromParPoint(om.cad.core.Point(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) Automatic conversions The python object model is very broad. For a single concept there can be different classes, each of which has its own field of use. Think for example of the concept of point, expressed in Coord3d, Point3d, Point3d and Point. We know that in python a function parameter can accept different types. In order to understand which types are accepted, we can relay on the type hints visible in the signature of the function itself. When working with the OM Python API you must remember that in addition to the types indicated in the function signature, you can also use all the types that are convertible into those explicitly indicated. How do you know if a type B is convertible into a type A? If A contains a constructor that has B as its only parameter, then to invoke a function f(A a) you can also use an instance of B as a parameter. For example, we have a method that require two parameters of type Coord3d. def func1(p1 : Coord3d, p2: Coord3d) You can create 2 objects of type Coord3d before call the method. p1 = Coord3d([1, 2, 3]) p2 = Coord3d([4, 5, 6]) func1(p1, p2) Instead, using automatic conversion it is possible to pass directly to the method the argument of the constructor and automatically the constructor will be called. So, our prevous snippet becomes: func1([1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]) Note: You can find which implicit conversion has a class reading the constructors that take only one parameter. For example, when a method requires a Vector3d it is also possible to pass a UnitVector3d because the Vector3d has the constructor that takes like parameters a UnitVector3d. Some automatic conversions are extremely. When a function expects a Material, Layer, or Workplane, you can pass the corresponding name to the function as a string. CAD Python API Below you will find a description of the main concepts necessary to be able to work with CAD bees. Keep in mind that we have already partially encountered many of the things necessary to interact with the CAD part of the document, i.e. all the functions of the om.commands package. However, many of the objects needed to use these functions are part of the cad. CAD Model The cad model is the entry point to inspec and modify the cad data. Through the CadModel object you have access to information on tag definitions, layers, workplanes and much more. -- 25 of 389 -- The example below shows how to extract layer information from the current document. Read layers app: om.Application = om.Application() document: om.Document = app.CurrentDocument cad_model: om.cad.core.CadModel = document.CadModel layers_manager: om.cad.core.LayersManager = cad_model.LayersManager # get the current layer current_layer: om.cad.core.Layer = layers_manager.CurrentLayer # get all layers layers: list[om.cad.core.Layer] = layers_manager.Layers # get a layer by name layer: om.cad.core.Layer = layers_manager.GetLayer("layer0") # read the layer name and description layer_name: str = layer.Name layer_descr: str = layer.Description Inside the cad model Layer are organized in a hierarchical structure within LayerContainer objects. A LayerContainer can in turn contain other LayerContainer. you can navigate the hierarchy to get all the information. For example, the function below allows you to know if a container is used, i.e. if it contains at least one used layer inside it. def is_container_used( layer_manager: om.cad.core.LayersManager, container: om.cad.core.LayerContainer ) -> bool: result = False childList = container.Children if len(childList) == 0: result = False else: children = container.Children for child in children: if isinstance(child, om.cad.core.Layer): if layer_manager.IsLayerUsed(child): result = True elif isinstance(child, om.cad.core.LayerContainer): result |= is_container_used(child) return result -- 26 of 389 -- CAD Entities The most important information of the CAD model is that relating to its entities, i.e. everything that is visible in the HM Model Structure window.
